title: Search Browser — a fast, light web browser for the Mac
excerpt: A free web browser for the Mac with nothing in the way: about 10 MB, open in a third of a second, ads blocked, Chrome extensions, Arc import.
content_html:
Search is a browser for the Mac with nothing in the way. About ten megabytes, the engine already in macOS, and a window that opens in a third of a second. Free, for any Mac on macOS 14 or later.

Version 1.0.14 · 10.8 MB · Free · Intel Mac?

It works: pick a tab, open a new one, swipe the tabs sideways for another space.

Two ways to hold it. Titles across the top, or down the side. The grey slides to the tab you pick either way, and a pinned site is one letter.

Spaces. Separate sets of tabs — work, home, a side project — each with its own icon. Two fingers sideways over the tabs and the next one slides in beside this one; past the last, a new one, signed in where you already are or starting afresh. Try it in the window above.

Read, watch, and nothing else. Reading mode keeps the article and its pictures, set to be read. Leave a video's tab and it follows you in a small window, above every app.

Light enough to forget it's there. Measured against Chrome and Safari on the same Mac, the same afternoon, the same pages. Medians of three runs; the method and every run.

10.8 MB on disk. No engine of its own to carry.

Search10.8 MB

Safari36 MB

Dia1,321 MB

Chrome1,429 MB

320 ms to the first window. Launched cold, no page open.

Search320 ms

Chrome526 ms

Safari730 ms

51 MB before the first page. Every process the app owns.

Search51 MB

Safari203 MB

Chrome663 MB

11 processes with five tabs open. Where Chrome runs 29.

Search11

Safari21

Chrome29

  • Pinned tabs. A letter at the head of the row. ⌘W puts it to sleep; it never leaves.

  • Ads blocked before they load. In the network layer — no scripts, no counter.

  • Hide anything. ⌘⇧H, click a thing, it's gone from that site for good.

  • Reading mode. The article, its pictures, nothing else. ⌘⇧R.

  • Floating video. Leave YouTube or Netflix and the video follows, above every app.

  • Passwords in your keychain. Shown with Touch ID. Passwords, bookmarks and history come over from Chrome or Dia in a click.

  • Spaces. Separate sets of tabs, each with its icon. Two fingers sideways to switch; stay signed in, or start afresh.

  • Chrome extensions. Straight from the Chrome Web Store, in a click. On macOS 15.4 or later.

  • A sidebar that steps aside. Tabs down the side or across the top. ⌘S folds the column away; the left edge brings it back.

  • Private tabs. ⌘⇧N. Its own cookies, no history, no place in tomorrow's session.

  • Web Inspector. Inspect Element on any page, the console at ⌥⌘J — WebKit's own tools.

  • Open source. The code is on GitHub — read it, build it yourself, or send a fix.

Questions? Answers.

A browser for the Mac by Office Commun, a design studio in Paris. Tabs, an address field, history, passwords, downloads — and as little around the page as we could manage. About 7 MB.

No. Search runs on WebKit, the engine that ships with macOS and powers Safari. That's why it's tiny: there's no second engine inside. Pages look exactly as they do in Safari.

Yes. No account, no subscription, and it's open source.

macOS 14 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. Intel Macs have a download of their own: Search for Intel, which updates itself from its own feed.

Yes. File › Bring Things Over… brings bookmarks, history, passwords and extensions from Chrome, Arc (its spaces too), Brave, Edge, Firefox, Zen and others, or from an exported file. macOS asks once for the other browser's key, and passwords land in your keychain under Search's name. Nothing in the other browser changes. Leaving Arc? Here is how it comes over.

Between your Macs, yes, if you turn it on: spaces, pins, bookmarks and a few settings go through a folder you choose, in iCloud Drive or Dropbox. No account, and never your history, passwords or sign-ins.

Every hour Search reads a small file on officecommun.com, signed by Office Commun; Search › Check for Updates… looks right away. If there's a newer build, it downloads it in the background, checks it was signed by Office Commun, swaps it in, and it's there next time you open Search. Settings, pins, history and passwords are never touched.

Settings › This Mac › Make it the default.

Yes: brew install --cask driceroland/tap/search. Search updates itself either way, and brew upgrade works too.
